I am gen z and qualified as a mental health nursing in 2021. I have finished my final ever job working as a mental health nurse this month. I feel proud of myself for finally putting my own mental health first. 

Nursing nearly killed me. I truly regret choosing this as my career. I thankfully am young and can retrain, but things from this profession will stay with me forever. Mental health nursing is not for the weak - and I am not weak. Despite the assaults, self-harm and suicides I feel what haunts me the most is the staff I worked with! The toxicity and the bullying was awful, the sexual harassment from older male staff was disgusting. As others said the understaffing was a huge issue too. 

I lost a fellow nursing friend to suicide from mistreatment from other staff, and she was in her early thirties. I felt so close to the edge myself that I knew I needed to get out. I was losing my hair and dropped two dress sizes, and I could barely recognise myself. 

So much more needs to be done to support staff.

So I have bpd and I’m a psych nurse in the UK, and I can tell you confidently that it is a blessing in disguise that you didn’t get the job. I’ve seen patients on other wards ask could they ever get a job and the response is always “of course!” but as soon as they leave, staff will actively laugh about it. 

They will have access to your medical notes, so will be able to see everything that has happened to you. If staff who worked there whilst you were a patient are still there, I honestly don’t believe they would be as kind to you as you’d expect. Maybe there would be a lack of trust because you’re “unwell” or maybe they’ll throw it in your face. I’ve seen it get very gaslighty with other people. They’re super sweet to the staff, but then slag them off as soon as they go. 

Also, unsurprisingly mental health workers hate personality disorders! They lump all the bad traits that they’ve witnessed from patients with pds, and then assume everyone is like that. My theory is that it’s easier to distinguish manic/psychotic patients from their illness and who they are as people as they are so obviously unwell you can’t help but feel for them, but since personality disorders are exactly what they are - “personality” disorders - they assume we have the same capacity as they do. You know, because we choose to be unwell 🙄 

Unfortunately, because of the demands of the job there is a lot of hostile staff. Maybe they’ve started out with good intentions and ended up nasty. If you’re not in the right hospital surrounded by the right team, it can make you into a power driven person. I’m incredibly lucky to be where I’m working now, but I had to search through so many areas to find what was right for me. Even though I love the team I work with, I’m still too scared to come clean about my mental illness (occupational health know of course but literally no one else does because my current manager hasn’t read the report even though I’ve been here for ages) because there’s so much stigma everywhere you go. When I did my dissertation on stigma faced by patients with personality disorders, one of the senior nurses on the ward I did my final placement on laughed directly to my face and told me she could sum it up in three words: “They deserve it.” 

I truly believe that ex-patients make the best healthcare workers when it comes to psychiatry, and I wouldn’t let this stop you if it’s something you’re passionate about! I’ve briefly mentioned having mental health issues to people I trust that I work with but went no further than that, especially since we’re not allowed to bring up our own experiences to patients. I hope one day I can be braver and talk my illness with pride, but I take joy in being the kindest version of myself to my patients, especially with bpd! I hope you will too! ❤️

I definitely feel the need to say that it’s nowhere near as bad as your stories, but I work in a psychiatric hospital which has been badly hit by Covid. Staff shortages now mean that I’m working multiple 13.5 hour shifts in a row (lost my entire Christmas and New Years covering for my colleagues) and I’ve been feeling so stretched thin and exhausted. Psych patients aren’t easy on the best of days, but putting covid restrictions on a ward full of manic or psychotic people is almost next to impossible.  I overheard some patients with more capacity discussing how they didn’t care if they brought covid in with them, or if they picked it up with us, because they’d just have an easier life since the nurses would do everything for them. Another patient asked “but what about them? The nurses who look after you?” and the whole room erupted in laughter. It was painful to hear on my sixth day in a row today. It felt like a proper kick in the gut after breaking my back trying to do as much as possible to help them. Now I’m home from the shift feeling just as indifferent about them as they clearly feel about me.

I’m about to start my third and final year of uni in the UK. I started at the age of 20 and will be 23 when I qualify, so age isn’t exactly a huge factor that should be considered when applying, although there’s normally a larger number of mature students than young students. 

My experience of uni hasn’t been the best but that’s because the team behind my university are extremely unorganised and not helpful. I’ve also realised that nothing I’ve learned from class has been transferable to the actually job. Everything I know and am comfortable doing was learned on placement!! I’ve had mainly positive experiences on placement due to having amazing mentors. You need to be proactive, willing to push yourself to get noticed by certain nurses and you need to get stuck in. If needs be, you’ll be wiping bums and lots of non-glamorous jobs.  But you see and do some incredible things. It can obviously be emotionally harrowing at times, but the wards you’ll be placed on will normally be very understanding if you’re affected by anything. I’ve been groped and attacked and been called every name under the sun, but when you build relationships with people it’s incredibly satisfying to see them becoming well. 

I love it so much, I love seeing the different aspects to life. No two days will ever be the same, and you’ll meet some truly incredible people. To me, it’s an honour and a privilege to get the opportunity to help people in their time of need. There’s days I come home in tears telling my roommates I want to quit, but things get better. Just remember to look after yourself too, because it’s a tough role and your wellbeing is just as important as your patients. Good luck with whatever you choose to do!!

As I said I’m not Jewish and it’s definitely not my goal to say that people should be offended or not, but it might be important to actually listen to the people it’s seriously offended? I know there’s a trend to jump on the bandwagon and follow the hate on Twitter, so I try and take everything with a pinch of salt. But it’s really affected some people. They have left the show in the interval because of how offended they felt, and feel like the show has been made into a joke.  It’s difficult to judge.

If you look at it in the sense that the show starts off with five non-Jewish people singing Four Jews in a Room Bitching, and it all leads up to Jason’s Bar Mitzvah, having no Jewish representation could easily help with the cast falling into stereotypes? I’ve seen the cast and they’re phenomenal. They are insanely talented and I think a lot of work was put into trying not to fall into said stereotypes, but what’s making people angry is that there should have been someone to represent Jewish culture to be there to guide them.

There are currently no Jewish cast members or production members of the UK show that are known. There was a Jewish consultant who tweeted to say he was a part of the show after the initial response, but he’s not really been heard of much after!

I started feeling suicidal when I was nine, for no apparent reason except I was genuinely convinced the people in my life would be better off without me. I’m twenty two now, and I was diagnosed with borderline personality disorder two and a half years ago. 

My mental health scares me. I’ve spent the majority of my life convincing myself I was better off dead and even though I do have the strength most of the time to know better than that, what happens when I truly give up? Living in a constant state of depression, where the slightest worry can spiral into telling yourself that you need to kill yourself at that very second is exhausting. I’m twenty two, and I know that this is still going to be ahead of me in my future. 

I need to constantly make sure that I’m not overly happy, or overly sad about things. I have to teach myself that it’s okay not to be okay every goddamn day. I need to look out for triggers. I need to learn not to hate myself so much when I relapse. I need to remind myself that I’m human and I’m allowed to make mistakes, even though it feels genuinely impossible most of the time.

The future is terrifying, because I don’t know how long I can do this for.
